extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on preparing and supporting 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter-eligibility rejections, including how to identify judicial exceptions in claims (Step 2A prong one), evaluate integration into a practical application (Step 2A prong two) and assess whether claims recite 'significantly more' (Step 2B), plus evidentiary and form-paragraph requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) the judicial exception and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection must explain why the claim limitations are considered judicial exceptions (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature). Where the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why it is an exception. See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information about Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea identification and grouping guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, provide justification under the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure if the limitation does not fall within enumerated groupings. The explanation may cite appropriate court decisions that support the identification but examiners should be familiar with cited decisions, avoid going beyond enumerated concepts, and avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match. Sample: 'The claim recites the step of comparing collected information to a predefined threshold, which is an act of evaluating information that can be practically performed in the human mind. Thus, this step is an abstract idea in the "mental process" grouping.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena identification
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify the law of nature or natural phenomenon as it is recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for more information. Sample: 'The claim recites the correlation of X, and X is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body, e.g., the naturally-occurring relationship between the presence of Y and the manifestation of Z.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature identification and markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.04(b) and § 2106.04(c) for the markedly different characteristics analysis. Sample: 'The claim recites X, which as explained in the specification was isolated from naturally occurring Y. X is a nature-based product... Because there is no indication... that isolation of X has resulted in a marked difference... X is a product of nature exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements and evaluate integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether they integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether (1) there are no additional elements in the claim, or (2) the claim as a whole, looking at additional elements individually and in combination, does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Give weight to all claimed additional elements even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements do not add 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When particular claim limitations are concluded to be well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support that conclusion in writing with one of the evidentiary options (A)-(D). Address additional elements both individually and in combination; a new combination of known steps may be eligible, so the examiner must consider combinations (Diamond v. Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05 for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only make a rejection if readily apparent and explain rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art in the Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so the applicant can effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why additional elements do integrate an exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer functions and computer-implemented claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind courts have found computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea where generic computer components are able in combination to perform functions that are not merely generic (e.g., DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for information about generic computing functions the courts have found to be mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer, and § 2106.05(d) for well-understood, routine, conventional activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and general linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding storing data to a mathematical computation does not add a meaningful limitation; placing a naturally occurring product into a generic container (test tube) is merely a nominal extra-solution component. Limiting an abstract idea to a particular industry may be insufficient (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) and 2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: consult and cite the specification to suggest claim amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice assists compact prosecution and gives applicants clear directions for overcoming eligibility rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary requirements — no evidence needed for Step 2A Prong One
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on external evidence such as publications or affidavits to find that a claim recites a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases show courts have identified abstract ideas without relying on evidence. Cf. Affinity Labs v. Amazon, OIP Techs. v. Amazon, Content Extraction & Transmission v. Wells Fargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary requirement when asserting well-understood, routine, conventional (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the exception is not integrated into a practical application or that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more, unless the examiner asserts that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, the examiner must find and expressly support the rejection in writing with one or more of the options (A)-(D) specified in Subsection III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support option (A): specification or applicant statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Support may be a citation to an express statement in the specification or to a statement made by an applicant during prosecution that demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification demonstrates well-understood, routine, conventional nature when it describes the additional elements as well-understood, routine, conventional (or equivalent), as a commercially available product, or in a manner indicating the element is sufficiently well-known that the specification need not describe its particulars to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A finding cannot be based only on silence in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support option (B): court decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Support may be a citation to one or more court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d) that note the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found to be well-understood, routine, conventional by the courts and recited at the same high level of generality. It is not enough that the elements are merely similar. Court decisions cited do not imply all computer functions are conventional; examiners must be careful in comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support option (C): publications demonstrating common use
rubrics_metrics.description: Support may be a citation to a publication (book, manual, review article, etc.) that demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publication must demonstrate that the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field—comparable to elements so well-known they need not be described to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A mere printed publication citation (e.g., a single patent) without demonstrating widespread prevalence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support option (D): official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Support may be a statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official notice only when the examiner is certain based on personal knowledge that the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant art. For example, taking official notice that a generic computer component performing a high-level generic function (like using the Internet to gather data) is well-understood, routine, conventional. Procedures for taking official notice and addressing applicant challenges are in MPEP § 2144.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs and required wording for §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified form paragraphs for §101 rejections: form paragraphs 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, and 7.05.016 (and 7.05.017 when a tentative abstract idea is involved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis, 35 U.S.C. 101) must precede the first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in all first actions and final rejections. ¶7.05 is a heading and must be preceded by 7.04.01 and followed by detailed explanation using appropriate paragraphs (e.g., 7.05.01, 7.05.016). ¶7.05.016 is for claims directed to a judicial exception without significantly more and applies to product and process claims; it requires filling brackets: [1] identify law of nature/natural phenomenon/abstract idea; [2] identify the exception as recited in the claim and why considered an exception (identify grouping for abstract ideas); [3] explain why combination of additional elements fails to integrate the exception into practical application; [4] explain why additional elements are insufficient to amount to significantly more. For tentative abstract ideas, include 7.05.017 and obtain the TC Director's signature.
